title: Pick the ripe tomatoes off the truss at the knuckle
instruction: Pick the ripe tomatoes off the truss and put them in the tray.
context: Picking tomatoes off the plant is one of the most familiar home-garden jobs: in the National Gardening Association's 2009 survey report, 31 percent of US households (about 36 million) grew food in 2008, and "the most popular vegetables grown include tomatoes (86 percent)"; its 2014 report counts 42 million food-gardening households in 2013. A ripe tomato is picked by bending it up and over at the knuckle, the joint on its stalk, until it snaps, which leaves the calyx on the fruit; pulling instead drags the stalk and the truss (a knuckle snaps at about 0.1 N m of bending but needs 40 to 72 N to pull apart, Weng et al. 2024). Green fruit is left to ripen, and the picked fruit must not be squeezed hard: ripe tomatoes show visible damage above about 30 N and their skin fails at 42 to 46 N (Guo et al. 2022; Kuta et al. 2023). Greenhouse pickers do the same all day.
setup: A table in front of two arms (bases 61 cm apart), seen by one overhead camera and a camera on each wrist. Positions are in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases: x forward (away from the arms), y to the robot's left; heights are above the table top. Tomato plant (fixed): a green stem 1.8 cm thick standing at x 37, y -6, and one truss: a peduncle 5 mm thick that leaves the stem 16.5 cm up, comes forward to x 31 and runs along y to y 24, falling 2.5 cm along the way. A pedicel 5 mm thick hangs from it 3 cm down to each tomato's knuckle (a small swelling). Tomatoes: three, 4.8 cm across and 60 g, centred 8.5 cm up at x 31 and y 3, 12 (red, ripe) and 21 (green, unripe); each has a green five-sepal calyx on top and a 12 mm stub of pedicel up to its knuckle. Each knuckle lets its tomato swing up to 35 degrees in any direction; bent further, it snaps (about 0.12 N m). Pulled along its stem, it holds and the pedicel stretches (about 1 mm per newton). Harvest tray (black plastic, fixed): 13 x 26 cm inside and 2.5 cm deep, centred at x 29, y 10, under the truss. The layout is the same in every trial, as in the screenshot.
scoring: Simulation, read every control step (20 Hz): a tomato is off the truss when its knuckle has moved 4 mm or more sideways from the end of its pedicel, and in the tray when it is off, its centre lies inside the tray's walls and its lowest point is within 3 mm of the tray floor (resting on it, not held above it). The squeeze on a tomato is the largest contact force (from PhysX) with which any link of either arm presses on it; a tomato pressed with more than 20 N at any time is crushed for the rest of the run. 0 for the rest of the run if the green tomato comes off the truss or is crushed, a tomato is pulled 6 mm along its stem (a 6 N pull on its 1,000 N/m stretch spring: the simulation's stand-in for a torn truss, as the simulated truss cannot tear), or a tomato falls onto the table outside the tray. Otherwise each red tomato earns the best it has reached, 0.25 once off the truss and 0.5 once off and in the tray, and nothing if it was crushed; the score is their sum, at most 0.75. 1.0: both red tomatoes in the tray, neither crushed, the green one still on the truss, both grippers at least 5 cm from every tomato, still for 1 s. Doing nothing scores 0. Real trial: score the same stages from the videos, then check right after the run. Photograph each tomato all round: a red tomato with split skin, a dent or flat spot, or juice showing earns nothing, and such damage on the green one scores 0. Inspect and photograph the truss: a torn, split or kinked peduncle or pedicel, a calyx left on the truss, or the green tomato off or hanging from a torn pedicel scores 0. A red tomato counts as picked only if it came off at the knuckle with its calyx and a short stub of stalk. In the tray means resting on its floor, not held; 5 cm with a tape measure.
reset_notes: On a real plant, use a fresh truss with two red and one green tomato for each trial. In the simulation a snapped knuckle stays snapped and a crushed tomato stays crushed for the run, so each trial starts the simulator afresh (each inspect-robots run does).
fidelity: Rigid bodies in Isaac Sim 6.1 (PhysX), 20 Hz control; plant, truss and tray fixed. Each knuckle is a ball joint, free within 35 degrees, that breaks past it at 0.12 N m; pulled, it never parts but stretches on a 1,000 N/m spring, and 6 mm (6 N) stands in for a torn truss, which the rigid truss cannot show. Tomatoes are rigid: no skin, bruising or juice; instead the PhysX contact force from the arms is read each step and over 20 N counts as crushed. Rolling resistance: spin damped.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (its right gripper went up to the truss beside the stem twice but took no tomato off; all three stayed on the truss); demo: 1.0
